tldr: By sampling multiple action chunks from a generative policy and continuously adapting joint stiffness and damping online according to their variation, the robot complies with human guidance when intention is ambiguous and provides firm assistance once the direction is clear.
hero_caption: Conceptual diagram of the proposed method. Multiple action chunks are predicted from camera images and external joint torques. When the destination is ambiguous and variation is large, the robot lowers stiffness to yield to the human. Once the direction is established and variation shrinks, it increases stiffness to assist transport firmly.
overview:
In physical human-robot interaction (pHRI), tuning joint stiffness (impedance) to decide when the robot should exert force and when it should yield to the human is critical. Keeping stiffness high throughout forcefully opposes unexpected human movements. Conversely, staying compliant all the time prevents the robot from providing sufficient physical assistance to carry heavy objects.

The authors focused on the intuition that at decision branch points where multiple future motions are possible, the variation among action predictions output by a generative model should increase. They built a CVAE (Conditional Variational Autoencoder)-based policy capable of sampling multiple future action chunks from images and joint torques. By computing the variance (deviation) across predicted actions, they directly link it to continuous online adjustment of joint stiffness and damping. Achieving compliance solely through internal signals of the action generation policy without an external intention estimator or role classifier makes the approach exceptionally smart.

Evaluated on a real 7-DoF robotic arm (Franka Research 3) in a four-direction collaborative transport task with a human, the proposed method achieved an average success rate of 0.95, significantly outperforming a fixed-stiffness ablation (0.83) and the deterministic FACTR baseline (0.69). At direction determination branch points, prediction variation surged as intended, making the robot compliant and allowing smooth guidance in the intended direction while preventing excessive torque collisions.
contributions: Proposed a generative policy that stochastically samples multiple future action chunks from images and external joint torques using an observation-conditioned prior
Developed a control framework that continuously adapts joint stiffness and damping online based on the variation (action deviation) among sampled action chunks

Achieved a 0.95 success rate in a real-world four-direction collaborative transport task, significantly surpassing fixed-stiffness and deterministic baselines while demonstrating reduced stiffness and interference torques at motion branch points

sections.heading: Human-Robot Collaboration: Compliant When Ambiguous, Firm When Decided
sections.summary: Collaborative tasks require providing firm assistance when intention is clear while remaining compliant when several future motions are plausible. This study presents an adaptive stiffness framework based on generative action-chunk sampling to continuously adapt robot compliance in real time.
sections.details:
In physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) such as co-manipulation or assembly, human movements vary from trial to trial. At decision points where the next direction is chosen, several future motions are plausible. If the robot maintains high stiffness, it forcefully resists unintended movements. If it stays compliant throughout, it cannot provide adequate physical support. A mechanism to continuously balance assistance and compliance online is essential.

Recent imitation learning methods have introduced Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to predict trajectory sequences, as well as contact-aware frameworks like FACTR. However, conventional ACT uses the fixed standard normal prior mean during inference, yielding deterministic outputs. Prior work has not generated multiple candidate actions online to link their variation directly to robot impedance.

This work combines FACTR-style multimodal inputs (RGB images and external joint-torque estimates) with an ACT-style CVAE architecture, extending the prior to be observation-conditioned. The model samples multiple future action chunks from current observations, using their variation as a proxy for uncertainty at motion branch points. High variation lowers stiffness to facilitate human guidance, while low variation increases stiffness for firm assistance, creating a closed-loop adaptive stiffness control system.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Contact-Rich Imitation and Variable Impedance Control
sections.summary: We review multimodal imitation learning for contact tasks, intention ambiguity modeling in HRI, and variable impedance control. The proposed method stands out by extracting stiffness adaptation signals directly from the generative action policy itself.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of three research lines:

- Multimodal policy learning for contact-rich interaction:
While classical behavioral cloning (BC) suffers from error accumulation, action chunking methods like ACT overcome this by predicting full trajectory chunks. Furthermore, FTACT and FACTR integrate force/torque information to capture contact states beyond vision. However, these methods either predict deterministic single trajectories or fail to link sample variation to physical compliance.

- Modeling intention ambiguity in HRI:
Because human motion involves redundancy and variability, approaches such as ProMPs and Interaction Primitives model trajectories probabilistically. Latent variable sequence models offer similar probabilistic perspectives, but utilizing distribution spread for low-level stiffness control rather than trajectory selection or classification has remained unexplored.

- Variable impedance control and role adaptation:
Dynamic adjustment of stiffness and damping is fundamental to safe pHRI. Recent works incorporate vision-language models (OmniVIC) or explicit leader-follower role estimation to modulate stiffness. However, these require dedicated models for task phase or role recognition. The key distinction of this work is extracting control signals directly from the generative action policy itself, achieving natural role adaptation without extra classifiers.

sections.heading: Turning Generative Sampling Variation into a Stiffness Control Signal
sections.summary: A Transformer CVAE model integrates images and external torques to sample multiple latent vectors from an observation-conditioned prior. Action deviation is computed from the time-weighted sample variance across decoded chunks to continuously interpolate joint stiffness and damping.
sections.details:
The overall architecture and mathematical formulation are as follows:

### Architectural Formulation
At time $t$, the model takes an RGB image $I_t$ and external joint-torque estimates $\tau_t$ to predict an action chunk of joint positions $\hat{q}_{t:t+k}$ over $k+1$ steps. A pretrained ViT extracts visual latent $z^V_t$ from the CLS token, while an MLP extracts force latent $z^F_t$. These are concatenated and passed through a Transformer encoder to produce context features $H^E_t$.
Like ACT, it is trained as a CVAE, but crucially, the prior distribution $p_\psi(z|H^E_t)$ is also predicted from $H^E_t$ via an MLP. During training, latent variable $z$ is sampled from posterior $q_\phi(z|H^E_t, q_{t:t+k})$ conditioned on the ground-truth chunk. During inference, $z$ is sampled from the observation-conditioned prior and passed to the Transformer decoder.

### Training Procedure
The loss function is a weighted sum of the reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}$ (L1 norm between predicted and ground-truth normalized actions) and the Kullback-Leibler divergence $\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}$ between posterior and prior (coefficient $\beta=1$). The curriculum learning strategy from FACTR is adopted to prevent over-reliance on force signals and overfitting to visual features.

### Action Deviation and Adaptive Stiffness Control
During inference, $M=10$ latent vectors are sampled from the prior and decoded into $M$ action chunks. For each step offset $\kappa$, unbiased sample variance is computed in normalized action space, and its square root gives action deviation magnitude $\sigma_{t+\kappa}$. Because branching impacts later steps more, linear weights increasing from $0.1$ to $0.9$ toward the chunk end are applied to yield the time-weighted deviation $\sigma_{t,\text{W}}$.

To smooth out high-frequency fluctuations from sensor noise, exponential moving average (EMA) smoothing ($\gamma=0.1$) is applied, followed by min-max normalization into $[0, 1]$ using empirical thresholds $\sigma_{\min}=0.061$ and $\sigma_{\max}=0.216$. The stiffness mixing ratio is computed as $\hat{\alpha}_t = 1 - \sigma_{t,\text{norm}}$. After passing through a slew-rate limiter (maximum step change $\Delta\alpha_{\max}=0.005$) to prevent jerky transitions, the ratio linearly interpolates between predefined high $(K_{\text{H}}, D_{\text{H}})$ and low $(K_{\text{L}}, D_{\text{L}})$ parameters to produce stiffness $K_r$ and damping $D_r$ matrices for a 500 Hz low-level controller. Execution commands use the most recent 30 steps from a single coherent sample combined via exponentially decaying temporal ensembling rather than the sample mean.

sections.heading: Real-World Evaluation in a Four-Direction Collaborative Transport Task
sections.summary: Using a 7-DoF arm, a collaborative transport task was designed where a human and the robot pinch a sponge block from both sides and carry it in one of four directions. The proposed method, a medium fixed-stiffness ablation, and deterministic FACTR were evaluated across 15 trials per direction (180 trials total).
sections.details:
Real-robot experiments were conducted to evaluate the proposed system.

### Experimental Setup and Task Sequence
The setup consists of a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 robotic arm and a front-facing Intel RealSense D435 camera. The manipulated object is a lightweight black laminated sponge block held solely by friction. Rather than grasping with a gripper, the human and robot pinch the block from opposite sides. The task proceeds in three phases:
- Approach and lift: The robot approaches the block side from its home position and lifts it to a predefined height together with the human. High stiffness is maintained as the trajectory is unambiguous.
- Direction determination and guidance: After lifting, the human applies force in one of four directions (forward, backward, left, right). Until transport begins, multiple destinations are plausible, causing prediction variation to surge so the robot lowers stiffness to accept guidance.
- Transport and assistance: Once the direction settles, variation drops and the robot re-engages high stiffness to provide firm tracking support.

### Data Collection and Implementation Parameters
The lead author performed all demonstrations and evaluation interactions. A total of 120 trials (30 Hz) were collected covering low/high stiffness settings and four directions (15 trials each). The dataset was manually split into 100 training trials and 20 offline validation trials for threshold calibration.
Policy inference runs at 7.5 Hz (every ~133 ms), generating 10 action chunks of 100 steps (~3.33 s). The low-level controller runs at 500 Hz. Success required reaching target displacements ($\ge 20$ cm for left, right, and backward; $\ge 15$ cm for forward due to workspace constraints). Safety torque trips or motion in incorrect directions were counted as failures.

### Baseline Conditions
The proposed method (stochastic policy + adaptive stiffness) was compared against an Ablation model (same stochastic policy with fixed medium stiffness) and a FACTR baseline (deterministic FACTR policy with fixed medium stiffness). Each condition underwent 15 trials per direction, totaling 180 online real-world evaluations.

sections.heading: Lower Stiffness at Branch Points Yields High Success and Reduced Torques
sections.summary: Latent space and joint trajectory analyses confirmed a sharp increase in prediction variation during direction determination. In real-robot experiments, the proposed method achieved a 0.95 success rate, significantly outperforming baselines in forward and right transport.
sections.details:
Key experimental findings include:

### Latent Space and Sampled Trajectory Variation Analysis
Analyzing the 16-dimensional latent space variance across offline validation sequences revealed that posterior variance remained near zero throughout. In contrast, prior variance surged around step 250 during direction determination, particularly along dimensions 8, 10, and 11.
Correspondingly, decoded chunks across all 7 joints displayed wide trajectory dispersion between steps 250 and 300, prominently on joints 1, 2, 4, and 7, confirming that the model captures multiple future possibilities.

### Success Rate Comparison in Real pHRI Experiments
Across all 180 evaluation trials, average success rates were 0.95 for the proposed method (57/60), 0.83 for the fixed-stiffness ablation (50/60), and 0.69 for the FACTR baseline (41/60).
- Forward direction: Exhibited the largest performance gap. While FACTR achieved only 0.27 (4/15) and the ablation achieved 0.67 (10/15), the proposed method reached 0.93 (14/15). In the two fixed-stiffness conditions, the robot resisted human pushing, frequently triggering emergency safety stops due to excessive joint torques. The proposed method dropped stiffness nearly to zero at the branch point, avoiding torque buildup.
- Right direction: The proposed method achieved 14/15, compared to 12/15 for both baselines. Failure analysis revealed that visual features near transport completion resembled those during direction determination, causing the model to mistake completion for a new branch and attempt returning. In the proposed method, this ambiguity also triggered low stiffness, allowing the human to easily hold the robot in place and recover from visual misclassification through physical compliance.

captions.F7: Control behavior comparison during forward transport. The proposed method (left) increases action deviation $\sigma_{t,\mathrm{norm}}$ around step 250, lowering stiffness and keeping torques low. In contrast, FACTR (right) suffers a sharp torque spike and triggers an emergency stop.

sections.heading: Implicit Role Adaptation and Current Limitations
sections.summary: The method realizes implicit role adaptation without separate modules. The authors discuss several limitations, including manual threshold tuning and the distinction between empirical action deviation and true statistical probabilities.
sections.details:
The system behavior can be interpreted as Implicit Role Adaptation dynamically shifting initiative between human and robot. Humans tend to stiffen their arms when facing unpredictable environments. When the robot compliantly softens in response, mutual fighting and oscillation are avoided. Achieving this 'yield when unsure, assist when confident' behavior directly from the action generation distribution—without extra task models or role optimizers—is a major practical advantage.

However, several limitations are highlighted:
- Thresholds $(\sigma_{\min}, \sigma_{\max})$ mapping deviation to stiffness were determined empirically from offline data and may need recalibration for new tasks or robot arms.
- Action deviation measures spread among candidate actions generated by the learned prior; it does not represent true human intention probability or epistemic uncertainty on out-of-distribution inputs.
- Experiments were conducted with a single participant (the lead author) in a four-direction transport setup, leaving generalization across diverse users and complex workflows for future validation.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook
sections.summary: We presented an adaptive stiffness pHRI framework leveraging action sampling variation from a multimodal generative policy. Future work will target out-of-distribution robustness and bidirectional active collaboration.
sections.details:
This paper presented an adaptive stiffness control framework for physical human-robot collaboration based on a generative action chunking model conditioned on RGB images and external joint torques. By leveraging variation among candidate actions sampled from an observation-conditioned prior to balance assistance and compliance, the approach demonstrated a 0.95 success rate with superior safety and ease of guidance in a four-direction transport task.

Future directions include:
- Incorporating explicit epistemic uncertainty estimation and fail-safe compliance strategies to handle out-of-distribution data and unforeseen disturbances.
- Expanding beyond passive compliance toward bidirectional collaborative systems with active, dynamic leader-follower role switching for more intuitive interaction.

takeaways: Sampling variation in a generative policy (CVAE) latent space serves as an effective online control signal for task branching uncertainty.
Directly coupling internal policy variance to low-level impedance enables smooth, implicit role adaptation without separate intention estimators or role classifiers.
Modulating stiffness to be compliant under high variation and firm under low variation avoids torque safety stops and allows easy human recovery from visual misclassifications.
limitations: Scaling thresholds (minimum and maximum deviation) for stiffness normalization are set empirically, lacking an automated calibration procedure.
Action deviation reflects candidate spreads learned from training data rather than true epistemic uncertainty on novel or anomalous inputs.
Real-robot validation was restricted to a single participant across a four-direction transport task, leaving multi-user and multi-task generalization unverified.
